name: Ngkolmpu
confidence_why: Carroll's 2016 reference grammar and his 2021 phonology chapter, the only first-hand descriptions of Ngkolmpu, mark stress on transcribed words but never state where it falls or what kind of system it is, and no other source (Donohue 2013, Evans 2021) fills the gap, so the record stands as undetermined on one describer's silence with nothing against it.

catalog_quote: This chapter sets out the phonemic inventory of consonants (2.1) and vowels (2.2) and describes their distribution and phonetic realisation. It establishes a set of phonotactic constraints (2.4) which are organised around a phonetic syllable structure. This structure is essential for describing the extensive process of epenthesis (2.4.1). The chapter also sets out the morphophonemic processes which interact with the phonotactics (2.5). The chapter concludes with a discussion of the orthography (2.6). ... [p. 65, infinitive prefix <o>] It is typically quite short and always unstressed. ... There is both phonological and syntactic evidence that these are not morphological compounds. Firstly, these are two distinct phonological units with individual stress for each word. ... The clitic never attracts stress and occurs within the intonation contour of the verb.

sources.quote: No sentence in the article states a stress, accent or tone system; the words stress, accent, tone, pitch, prominence, prosody and intonation do not occur. Stress is shown only in the phonetic transcriptions, which carry a primary-stress mark on every transcribed word, e.g. (22) a. /t-rowrt/ -> [ˈtrɔ.wə̆rtʰ] '(He) follows (him)'; b. /næmpr-t/ -> [ˈnæ.mpʰərtʰ] 'one at a time'; c. /s-rtrow-ŋk/ -> [sər.ˈtɾɔʷŋk] '(He) destroyed (it)' (p. 48, IPA glyphs read from the extracted text rendering); and in prose: 'The variety described in this paper is Ngkontar with all data drawn from firsthand fieldwork in Yanggandur.' (p. 33); 'The unrestricted maximal syllable structure for Ngkolmpu is [CCVC], extended to [CCVCC] in word-final syllables. The minimal syllable structure is [CV].' (p. 47); 'Vowels are typically lengthened in open monosyllabic words without codas, although this is only a tendency.' (p. 45)

sources.note: The phonology chapter (ch. 2, pp. 27-62: consonants, vowels, underspecified phonemes, phonotactics, morphophonemics, orthography) has no section on stress, accent, tone or prosody, and the thesis nowhere states a stress rule; 'tone' does not occur in the text. Stress is presupposed: one stress per phonological word (p. 117), the topic clitic and the infinitive prefix are unstressed (pp. 120, 65). sources.note: Areal overview of the eight languages in LD&C SP24 (Yelmek, Ngkolmpu, Nmbo, Nen, Idi, Ende, Bitur, Urama); Sota Kanum [krz] is not in the sample -- the Kanum-group language covered is Ngkontar Ngkolmpu [kcd, ngka1235] (Glottolog: Yam > Kanum > Ngkrn-Ngkantr > Ngkantr; Sota Kanum sits directly under Ngkrn-Ngkantr). P.7 states that SNG phonologies share no positive typological features, only absences: 'no tone, no pitch accent or distinctive stress except for Urama'. Bears on Sota Kanum only as sister-language/areal evidence.
